Yes, 3.44 is post-100% tech-debt work. The plan was covering your docs question but not the graph, so I've added a task for the graph.

**What was already planned:**
- **Day-1 guide and retrospective (T11).** The phase-close docs task writes the 3.44 lesson into the day-1 guide: measure each function's signature from the machine code, not from the C. It also extends the retrospective, story and wiki to Phase 44.
- **3.43's naming lessons (T13).** The task we added earlier backfills these into the day-1 guide and adds the names chart.

**What was missing: a chart for this phase's work.** The plan was approved before rule T5, which says a new kind of work gets its own chart. The only existing chart that touches signatures counts wrong return types, and that's just one of the six kinds of disagreement 3.44 fixes. So I've added a task. It runs after the milestone check, at the next task boundary, so T10 isn't disturbed. It does three things:
- **A signatures chart in the README.** It counts the disagreements left of each kind and the recorded exceptions. It starts from T4's 198,029 and shows each fix-up task's drop, where that task's summary gives the number.
- **A prevention lesson in the day-1 guide**, beyond the "what happened" lesson. A new decomp would:
  - keep one shared prototype header from the start;
  - check every signature against the machine code from the first matched function;
  - ban empty `()` and old-style declarations;
  - mark and record every cast that changes how a call is read.
- **The same point** in the retrospective's "what to do sooner" part.

**One ordering note.** We meant T13's names chart to land before the milestone check, so the check's snapshot would include it. It didn't run first, so it runs right after T10 and writes its own first row instead. Nothing is lost; the milestone row just won't have the names columns.

The milestone check (T10) is running now: the full rebuild passed 218 of 218, and the 22-minute health check is under way.

- A name is cited only from a recorded source, and every name a model words is a marked `guess_` with its basis, confidence and evidence kind.
- Placeholders are per binary, so the rename tool must work one binary at a time before the first rename.
- Every scan gets a time limit, with its patterns joined into one expression per chunk (C0575).
- Count how many names have outside evidence before planning a naming phase.

Chapter 10 gets one matching honesty rule. The wiki pages Start-a-new-decomp-project and How-to-AI-decomp point to item 5 and to the Naming conventions section.

Each unit is counted as cited (it has a cited row in `config/names.tsv`), guess (`guess_`), other (named but with no ledger row) or placeholder; the four add up to the total, and the tool checks that.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Functions | 92,486 | 513 | 285 | 228 | 91,460 |

Files that missed the walk cache were put into `results` first. Files that hit the cache were then assigned with `results[rel] = r`, which keeps each key's existing position. So `results.values()` listed the misses before the hits, and which files missed depended on which mtimes had changed. `build_struct_map` (:798-860) feeds its union-find from that order. The union-find refuses some merges (a width conflict, or no shared offset) depending on what was merged earlier, so a different order gives different clusters. A second, smaller difference: fresh walks were plain Python objects while cached ones had been through JSON. **Fix.** Commit 23125e7899. I used a fixed order rather than a content-keyed cache, so the output no longer depends on cache state at all. - `walk_all` now builds `results` in the sorted `files` order. - A new `_walk_worker_json` puts fresh walks through the same JSON round trip as cached ones. `_walk_worker` itself is unchanged, because restruct.py calls it directly. - The docs/struct-map.md stamp now carries only the commit, not the wall-clock time. Phase 3.44 is finished and needs your word to close it. Its milestone check passed in full. All 218 game files still rebuild byte-identical, and all six Ghidra proofs pass.

**What the phase did.** It answered your 11-10 concern: matching bytes never proved that each function's declaration tells a modder the truth. Every declaration and definition now agrees with what the original machine code actually does. Where the shipped game itself was inconsistent, the exception is on record with the exact instructions that prove it.
- **A signature census** (`tools/sig_evidence.py`) reads the machine code of all 218 game files in about 17 seconds. For each function it records:
  - whether callers use the return value;
  - how many arguments it takes;
  - how wide each value is.

  Each answer cites its instruction. Where the code can't decide, mostly calls through function pointers, it says "unknown" and why.
- **198,029 disagreements went to 0 unaccounted for**, fixed in four tasks:
  - **wrong return widths (T5):** the count first grew from 27 to 116 functions once the hidden declarations were counted;
  - **empty `()` declarations (T6);**
  - **392 non-void functions with no `return` (T7):** each now has a real return, `void`, or a comment saying what the return register holds;
  - **the rest (T8):** `void` functions whose result is read, wrong argument counts, and our declarations of Sony's library functions, now matching Sony's own headers.
- **Two marked casts.** Where the shipped game read a call differently from the function's real prototype, the call now goes through `RET_AS` or `KR_AS`. That covers about 1,500 and 2,250 calls. Each is backed by a recorded exception whose cited instructions the check re-verifies against the original bytes.
- **What's still recorded as exceptions:** 3,264 rows. Most are `()` declarations in shared headers that serve overlays whose definitions disagree, so no single prototype fits.
- **A permanent gate.** The health check now fails on any new disagreement that isn't recorded. That adds about 90 seconds to its 21 minutes.
- **The struct map's counts** no longer vary from run to run (T2).
- **The scratch-compile check** that coders kept re-copying is now a tool (`tools/scratch_cmp.py`), ready for 3.45's struct merges.
- **Docs and charts:**
  - The README has two new graphs: names (cited, guesses and placeholders left) and signatures (the 198,029 down to 0).
  - The day-1 guide has 3.43's naming lessons and 3.44's prevention lesson: one shared prototype header, the signature check from the first matched function, no `()` declarations, and every view cast recorded.
  - The story, retrospective and wiki run to Phase 44. The wiki also has a modder's guide to reading the census.

**Left open:**
- **Cleared shared-function rows.** 88 of the shared-function exceptions recorded for differing return types are now cleared, so those functions can be merged into one shared source. T10 suggests pointing that item at the file-layout phase, 3.46, rather than 3.45. I'd do that.
- **One more varying count.** The lever census has the same run-to-run counting bug that T2 fixed in the struct map. It's a small fix for a later phase.
- **The live-memory session** for confirming names is still owed to you.

**After the close:**
- I restart the MCP Ghidra, and you run `/mcp`.
- You push the repo and the archive clone (archive commit 05feeb4).

The close question is open in the picker.

Phase 3.44 is closed. I've started the planner for Phase 3.45, and I'll open its draft in the plan view when it's ready.

**What 3.45 is for.** Your instinct on 11-12 was right: the game has a few hundred real structs, not 14,000. The 14,376 is the census's count of partial views of structs. The headers hold about 3,400 struct definitions, about 3,100 of them still placeholders named `Unkstruct_…`, and many are just pieces of the same real struct. 3.45 merges those pieces into the game's real types and names them, so modders see an actor struct or a camera struct instead of fragments. It also unlocks the file-layout phase (3.46), which can then name files and headers after real systems.

**What it builds:**
- **A count first.** It measures how many placeholder structs there are and what evidence links them, so the target number comes from measurement, not a guess.
- **Rename tools for types and fields.** Today's tools can rename only functions and data, which is why 3.43 left structs out.
- **The merges.** Every placeholder struct is settled one of three ways:
  - merged into its real type, on evidence: a shared global, a pointer passed between functions, shared code, or matching field widths in the machine code;
  - kept apart, with a written reason;
  - left alone, with a recorded "no evidence" note.

  A tool checks that none is left unsettled. Structs that merely look alike are never merged.
- **Names.** The surviving types get names, and so do the fields of the most-used ones. Each name is cited or marked `guess_` with its basis, as in 3.43.
- **A chart.** A struct series and README graph, under rule T5.
- **Maybe a small fix.** The lever census's counts vary from run to run, the same bug T2 fixed in the struct census. I've asked the planner to include the fix if it's cheap.

**What it must not change:**
- the game's bytes: all 218 files still rebuild byte-identical, checked object by object with the new scratch-compile tool;
- function signatures, except where a merge changes a parameter's type, and 3.44's signature check re-checks those;
- file locations: no file moves until 3.46.

**How big it is.** Judgment-heavy, like 3.43. Each merge needs evidence, and changing a widely used header recompiles thousands of objects, so the work goes in batches. The planner sizes it from the count.

The draft will most likely ask once more to stop Ghidra for the proofs.

- **Push** the repo, and the archive clone at `/home/musashi/BFM-decomp-archive` (commit 05feeb4).

The Phase 3.45 plan is in the plan view. Two things in it need your decision.

**1. Stopping Ghidra once, at the milestone check (T11).** It's needed for the six proofs and to load the renamed types into your live Ghidra project, after a backup. Ghidra would stay off until the close, then I restart it and ask you for `/mcp`. **I recommend yes**, the same as in the last four phases.

**2. A gap the planner found in what 3.44's signature check covers.** We assumed the check would catch a struct merge that changes a function parameter's type. It doesn't. It compares return types and argument counts, not the types of the arguments, so a declaration that names the wrong struct for a parameter would pass unnoticed. The plan adds that check in T8: each struct parameter in a declaration must name the same struct as the function's definition. T2 measures it first, then it's gated at 0 unaccounted for. **I recommend yes.** Without it, the merges' effect on prototypes would go unchecked, which is exactly the risk we deferred to this check.

**One choice to know about now, though it's settled at T2's review.** The plan names every surviving type, but only the fields of the 20 most-used types. Changing that 20 means changing the milestone, and that's yours to decide when T2 brings the measured numbers.

Since the plan view doesn't record answers, I'll take your approval of the plan as a yes to both, as before.

## Rationale
- Order: baselines and the inventory (T1); the evidence census and the developer's word on the proposed dispositions and the naming scope (T2, review); the rename tooling for types and fields (T3, runs while T2 waits); lever_census's cache order (T4, before any batch compares its output); the struct series and README graph (T5, so every task-close snapshot records the fall); the fold engine and pilot (T6); the fold batches (T7); the apart and no-evidence dispositions and the gate (T8); type names (T9); field names (T10); milestone gate (T11); close docs (T12, rule T5); cleanup (T13).
- Measure first (DECIDED): T1 and T2 change no source. T2's review is where the developer sees the real numbers before any fold: links per evidence class, components, projected survivors, conflicts and size vetoes, DECL-PARAM, the naming scope; he picks stop rules once buckets exist (card). After his word Claude adjusts T7, T9 and T10 with plan_edit (sizes, splits, scope) inside the milestone.
- Rename tooling first (DECIDED; R110): the folds retype their users through kind `type`, so T3 precedes T6, and the names (T9, T10) use both kinds. The field path is compiler-proven (Context), never a text rewrite.
- One tool for the inventory, the evidence and the gate: prefer extending tools/struct_twins.py (it binds type names to globals, locals, parameter slots and returns, R3.45-003) and type_census's walk. If a new tool is needed, §3's three lines go in T1's summary; the planned ones: what it does (links placeholder types by the four evidence classes, proposes and gates their dispositions); what exists (type_census clusters cast bases, struct_twins binds tier-2 layout twins only, restruct folds by layout and name, leverage_rank has reach(T)); the delta (links between declared types of different layouts, a disposition ledger and its check).
- The disposition ledger: one tracked row per placeholder at T1's HEAD (default config/struct_dispositions.tsv; the expert names it): type, disposition (undisposed, fold, apart, no-evidence), target, evidence class, cites, cause or reason, task. Type renames follow into it (T3). docs/struct-twins.md's apart section is generated from it, so the doc and the ledger cannot drift.
- Deterministic links (C0582): fixed input order and stable tie-breaks; two runs on one tree give the same components and targets. A component's target is its real type when it has one (an SDK type its value is passed to, a ledgered name), else the member with the largest reach(T), ties by name.
- DECL-PARAM (Developer decides 2): a declaration whose struct parameter names another type than its definition is evidence class (2), measured in T2. After the folds, T8 adds the rule to sig_evidence so the signature gate sees parameter types; disagreements the folds leave are ledgered with their cause, never edited (scope: prototypes touched only by a fold).
- Effort: T2 is the one `effort: high` task: what counts as a link in each class, when a component is safe to fold (width conflicts, load-bearing sizes, hub slots) and how a target is chosen are judgments no test fully arbitrates, and every fold copies them. Its selftest proves the mechanics; the review judges the rest.
- Name scope (milestone "the surviving types and the fields of the top types by leverage named, cited or guess_"): every surviving type, and every accessed field of the top 20 surviving types by reach(T), is cited or `guess_`; none is left no-evidence, since its accesses always give a basis to quote, and a thin basis gives a low-confidence guess (card: a prefixed best guess beats a bare placeholder). pad<HEX> bytes are never accessed and never named. T2's review shows both counts; moving the 20 or capping the types amends the milestone and is the developer's word.
- Series (rule T5, DECIDED): struct consolidation is a new kind of work, so it gets its own readability columns and README graph (T5), early, so the task-close snapshots record the fall; T12 regenerates and publishes it.
- lever_census (Claude's call (a)): the 3.44 T2 fix, about 5 lines at lever_census.py:858-876 (R3.45-004); every batch compares lever_census output, so it lands before the folds (T4).
- Ghidra: the repo mirror (config/ghidra/types/) is regenerated with every batch, since tools-health runs `ghidra_types.py --check`; the six --proof legs and the live type import need :8080 free, one stop at T11 (Developer decides 1).

## Cookbook

## Developer decides
- The MCP Ghidra is running and serves port 8080 (planner check 2026-11-13). The six Ghidra proofs and the live type import need that port free. Recommended: approve now one clean stop with tools/ghidra_mcp_stop.sh when T11 (the milestone gate) starts; it saves, then stops, never kills, as in R49, R91, R108 and R146. While it is stopped, T11 also imports the folded and renamed types into your live project after a backup (C0554), so your Ghidra shows the new names. It stays stopped to the close; then Claude runs tools/ghidra_mcp_start.sh and asks you for /mcp. Until T11 it keeps running for your use; no other 3.45 task needs it stopped.
- The signature gate does not check parameter types. sig_evidence compares return types, parameter counts and argument words only (tools/sig_evidence.py:1217-1267; docs/ops/sig-evidence.md:204-207), so "re-checked by 3.44's signature gate" would not catch a declaration whose struct parameter keeps another type than its definition. Recommended: T8 adds one rule, DECL-PARAM (a declaration's struct-typed parameter names the definition's struct type), to sig_evidence --compare and --check, measured first in T2 (where such disagreements are fold evidence) and gated at 0 unledgered; disagreements the folds do not resolve are ledgered with their cause, never edited. Cost: one rule, a selftest and its ledger rows inside T8. If you decline, folds rely on rename_scan's 0 stale old-type tokens and R22, and no gate checks parameter types; Claude then drops part (3) of T8 with plan_edit.

## Risks
- The evidence may link far fewer types than "a few hundred real types" suggests, leaving many no-evidence placeholders: the milestone still holds (no-evidence is a disposition), the survivor count is reported as measured, and T2's review sets the naming scope; nothing is folded on a look-alike to reach a number.
- Over-merging: links are transitive, and one wrong link (a generic buffer pointer, a void *-like slot, a callee whose parameter receives many unrelated types, a pool or list helper) can merge unrelated types. T2 refuses hub slots, names them, and the review sees the largest components.
- Width conflicts and sign mixes inside a component (773 census clusters carry one today): a fold needs one width and sign per accessed offset; a conflict keeps the members apart (the cause cites both accesses) unless a union member reproduces both views byte-identically.
- Load-bearing sizes: a fold that grows a type changes sizeof, array strides, pointer arithmetic and struct copies; such a fold keeps the size or is refused; R22 catches what the static check misses.
- Controls: folds or renames touching MATRIX_L48, Prim_8016E7C8 or D_800A651C's types move type_census controls 2-4 (type_census.py:1694-1715); the task re-points the control in the same commit with the reason, never to make a failure pass.
- Generated blocks: once retired, include/struct_types.h is hand-maintained; a later run of head_types.py or `restruct.py --decide-band --write` would clobber the folds unless both refuse (T6).
- Spelling-keyed tools (C0572): a type rename silently drops types from leverage_rank (:450), restruct (99 mentions), type_census and the 3.40 configs (type_folds.tsv, tnc_band.tsv) unless each follows; T3 proves census-neutrality before and after a pilot rename.
- Field renames: a field name is not unique (unk10 in hundreds of types), so a text rewrite renames other types' fields. Only the compiler-proven path (owner-typed accesses, 0 "has no member named", identical objects) is allowed; a member spelled inside a SHARED_FN body or a common.h macro is checked at every expansion.
- Cost: every header edit rebuilds the fleet: R22 per batch (about 4 min alone), type_census (about 6 min) and `struct_twins --write` per batch, tools-health (about 21 min) at each task end.
- The live import replaces type rows in the developer's Ghidra project: C0554's backup first, the program-row guard, the export cmp; never the full merge output (it re-applies committed function and comment rows over live edits).
- Ledger drift: the disposition ledger, docs/struct-twins.md, names.tsv and the types worklist move in the same commit as each batch; the gate re-verifies cites against the current tree, so a later edit that removes a cited line fails it until the row is updated.
- Disk: 24 GB free; scratch baselines and worktrees take a few GB each; each task deletes its own (T13 checks).

review

T2 is finished and waiting for your review. Every one of the 4,112 placeholder struct types now has a proposed disposition built only on cited evidence: 202 fold into another type, 1,004 are kept apart with a cause, and 2,906 have no evidence either way. That leaves 3,910 surviving types. Nothing in src/ or include/ changed.

**What the tool does.** T1's tool, `tools/struct_twins.py`, has a new `--links` mode. It links two types only when one of these holds:
- **Shared global:** the same object (same binary and address) is declared with both types.
- **Pointer passed:** a value of one type reaches a slot of the other. This includes a `void *` or scalar parameter that its routine always casts to one type.
- **Shared routine:** the same routine, copied into several overlays, types the same slot differently in different copies.

A link is refused when:
- the two types disagree on a field's width or sign at an accessed offset;
- a size that matters (arrays, `sizeof`, pointer arithmetic, copies) differs;
- it passes through a generic helper or header type (a "hub").

Joins go through the .d files and the ELF symbol tables, never a bare name. Two runs on one tree give identical output. `--selftest` passes 17/17, including the four planted cases the plan asked for. tools-health is OK.

**What it found.**
- **The evidence does not support "about 50 real types".** 2,639 placeholders appear only as casts of untyped values, with nothing linking them to any other type.
- **Plain typed flows carry almost no evidence:** only 26 call arguments pass one struct type into a parameter of a different one; the cross-type evidence lives in untyped slots, shared globals and routine copies.
- **Declaration parameter check (DECL-PARAM): 0 disagreements** across 61,137 placed declaration/definition pairs. Separately, 20,816 pairs have a struct on one side and `void` or a scalar on the other; they are counted apart and are not DECL-PARAM.
- **Twins:** of the 452 listed twin classes, 45 are now linked, 5 are split and 402 stay apart.
- **One large component needs judgment:** 53 types gather on Unkstruct_800B5CB8, which earlier work already flagged as a suspect merge of several real types.

**Decisions in the Review block, with my recommendations:**
1. **Evidence policy:** use "effective" (202 folds). The "views" policy adds only 8 folds, through cast spellings that can be codegen levers.
2. **Accept the measured outcome:** keep the evidence bar rather than folding look-alikes.
3. **Hold B4**, the 53-type component on 800B5CB8. T7 should first tighten the hub-type test and re-propose, which turns its 52 members into "apart".
4. **T7 fold batches:** B1 is 90 folds from shared globals and routine copies, B2 is 50 pointer folds, B3 is 10 folds in 2 larger components. Each batch is one commit with R22 run alone. A failing component goes back to "apart" with its cite. Stop after 2 refused components in one batch, or any type_census control move.
5. **Naming scope for T9:** name the 930 survivors with reach 2 or more, plus every fold target, and defer the 2,980 with reach 0 or 1 to Gen 4. This narrows the milestone, so it is the developer's call; the alternative is `guess_` names for all 3,910.
6. **Fields for T10:** keep the top 20 survivors by reach.
7. **Field style:** confirm lowerCamelCase fields, `guess_` outermost with a basis row, and the citation beside the `/* 0xNN */` offset.
8. **Scope boundary:** confirm the 4,112 placeholders, PsyQ's 14 excluded.
9. **DECL-PARAM:** T8 adds the rule as a guard at 0 (R179).
10. **`(void *)` casts at a call:** accept them as pointer evidence.

**How it got here.** Five coder runs, each fixing what the previous run exposed:
- a scoping bug that mis-bound every `a0` parameter in one file (c2);
- a 112-type star built through per-overlay copies of helpers, fixed by treating copies of one routine as one slot (c3, c4);
- width checks that could not see cast-only types (c5).

I made two small edits to the hub test myself: routine-copy links now go through the same helper test, and two header types can never merge. Five lessons are banked in the cookbook (C0604–C0608).

The Review block's edits are four `plan_edit.py append-change` lines for T7, T9 and T10.

T2 needs your review. T2 measured every placeholder struct and proposed what to do with each one, and the result is not what we expected.

**What it found.** There are 4,112 placeholder structs. T2's tool looked for evidence that two of them are the same real struct: a shared global, a pointer passed from one function to another, or shared code. It was checked twice with identical output, and its self-test passes.
- **202 can be merged** into another type on that evidence.
- **1,004 are kept apart**, each with a recorded reason.
- **2,906 have no evidence either way.**

That leaves **3,910 types after merging, not a few hundred.** The reason is that 2,639 of them aren't really struct definitions. They are one-off casts, where a function reads one or two fields through a pointer that nothing else links to. They may well be pieces of the same real structs, but nothing in the code proves which. Merging them because they look alike is exactly what our rules forbid, because a wrong merge gives a modder a false type. **I recommend accepting the number as measured and keeping the evidence bar.** The real count of game structs is still likely in the hundreds; we just can't prove the links for the small fragments.

**The decisions:**
1. **How strict a merge's evidence must be.** The middle setting gives the 202 merges. The loosest adds only 8 more, through casts that may be compiler tricks rather than real links. **Use the middle setting.**
2. **Hold one suspicious merge.** A group of 53 types all joins onto one struct, `Unkstruct_800B5CB8`. The struct map already flagged that as a likely false merge through a shared hub. **Hold it.** T7 first teaches the tool to spot the hub, then measures again.
3. **How the merges run (T7).** Three batches of 90, 50 and 10 merges, one commit each, with the full 218-file rebuild after each. A merge that changes the bytes goes back to "apart" with the reason, and the batch continues. T7 stops and reports after 2 such failures in one batch. **Yes.**
4. **How many types get names (T9). This one changes the milestone, so it's yours.** The milestone says every surviving type gets a name.
   - **The expert's proposal, and mine:** name the 930 types used in 2 or more places, plus every merge target. The 2,980 used in 0 or 1 places keep their placeholder names and ledger rows, and wait for Gen 4.
   - **The alternative:** give all 3,910 a `guess_` name with a basis row. That matches your "a best guess beats a bare placeholder" preference. But for a one-field cast seen once, the guess would mostly restate its address and size, and it would make T9 several times bigger.
5. **Field names (T10):** the fields of the top 20 types, as planned. **Keep 20.**
6. **Name style:** types in PascalCase, fields in lowerCamelCase, `guess_` on the outside (`guess_posX`), with the basis in a comment beside the field's offset. **Confirm.**
7. **Scope:** the 4,112 placeholders, with Sony's 14 library structs left out. **Confirm.**
8. **The new parameter-type check:** it found 0 disagreements. T8 still adds it as a guard. **Yes.**
9. **A `(void *)` cast passed into a typed parameter counts as pointer evidence.** **Accept.**

The picker is open. If you approve, I'll record these in the plan, mark T2 done, and T3 starts.

I've counted the structs in the Castlevania: Symphony of the Night decomp myself, from a checkout of its headers and source. That's the most mature community decomp of a 1997 PS1 game.

| Where | Struct and union types |
|---|---|
| Shared headers | 707 |
| Inside source files | 570 |
| **Total** | **about 1,280** |

- **402 of the header structs are per-enemy layouts.** They use one shared actor struct and lay each enemy's own data over its spare area.
- **63 still carry placeholder names**, years into that project.

So a real game of this era looks like several hundred to about a thousand types, not 50 and not 4,000. Our 3,910 is clearly too many. Your 200 is probably a little low.

Their contributor guide also explains how they got there. They type the pointer: a function that gets an enemy is declared to take the actor struct, so every field read becomes a field of that one struct. Where enemies differ, they use per-enemy overlays rather than separate fragment structs. When unsure, they leave a thing unnamed rather than name it wrongly.

No other PS1 Square decomp (FF7, Legend of Mana, Silent Hill, Metal Gear Solid) publishes a struct count or a merging guide.

The measurement of our own shapes is still running. When it lands, I'll put the revised struct merge plan and my view on effort in front of you.

T2 needs your decision. I measured the structs; here is what the data says and a revised plan for finishing all of them in Gen 3.

**Your instinct is right, with one correction.** Most of the 4,112 placeholders aren't real structs at all.
- **1,714 have only one or two fields.** They're fragments: a function reads one value through a pointer that has no type, so the tool invents a tiny struct just for that read.
- **They fit almost anything.** About three-quarters of the small fragments fit inside more than five of the larger structs, and only 5 to 10% fit exactly one. For example, 50 placeholders are just "a 2-byte value at offset 2". Shape can't tell you which real struct a fragment belongs to.

So "same shape, same struct" is sound for full structs, but not for one- or two-field fragments.

**How SOTN gets the count down.** The Castlevania: Symphony of the Night decomp has about 1,280 struct types. It doesn't merge fragments by look; it gives the pointer a type. A function that gets an enemy is declared to take the actor struct, so every field read becomes a field of that one struct and the fragment disappears. For us, 1,135 fragments come from exactly that case: a function argument with no type, always cast to the same struct.

**Why earlier phases didn't finish.** I counted what Gen 3 left undone.
- **Not effort, as far as the records show.** No record says work stopped because effort ran out.
- **Mostly the stop rules.** "0 unaccounted" let a recorded exception count as finished, and at those stops the narrower option was offered and taken.

The fix I'd make is the finish line, not just the effort level.

**The revised plan for 3.45:**
1. **Merge exact twins of three or more fields on shape alone.** That removes about 830 types, and those twins are almost certainly the same struct.
2. **Merge the small shared value shapes into one type each.** These are things like a four-short vector or an 8-byte block. Around 40 groups like that become one shared type each, such as a `Vec4s`, much like SOTN uses Sony's `SVECTOR` everywhere.
3. **Absorb the fragments by tracing their pointers, one by one.** This is your hand-cracking idea, and I agree with it. A tool lists each fragment's candidate parent structs and where its pointer comes from. Coders then read each case, in batches like the function-cracking waves, and give the pointer its real type, so the fragment becomes a field of its parent.
4. **A new finish line: zero `Unkstruct_` placeholders left.** Nothing goes to Gen 4.
   - A merge is only refused if it changes the game's bytes, and only after a second attempt with the usual compiler tricks.
   - Every surviving type gets a name: cited, or `guess_` with its basis.
   - Fields are named for the most-used types.
5. **Effort.** The experts for the judgment tasks (twin review, fragment tracing, naming) run at high effort on Fable, and the coders on high.
6. **The old T2 proposals are dropped.** The hub group T2 wanted to hold is judged in step 3 rather than held.

**What it costs.** This is a much bigger phase: probably several thousand judgments, several waves, and many full rebuilds. I'd split it into two phases, consolidation (3.45) and names (3.46). File layout and the rest would move down by one. The phase plan gets redrafted by a fresh planner, and you approve it again in the plan view.

**I recommend yes.** The picker is open.

**Why it's changing.** The old plan would have left almost 3,000 placeholder structs for Gen 4. The new one finishes the job in Gen 3. Its finish line is zero placeholder structs left. A merge can be refused only if it changes the game's bytes, and only after a second attempt with the usual compiler tricks.

**What the new 3.45 does:**
- **Merges exact twins.** Structs with three or more fields and the same layout are merged on shape alone, about 830 of them. That changes our old rule that structs which merely look alike stay apart.
- **Gives small repeated shapes one shared type each.** Things like four-short vectors and small byte blocks become one type per shape. Where Sony already has a matching type, such as `SVECTOR` or `RECT`, we use Sony's.
- **Traces the one- to five-field fragments by hand.** This works like the function-cracking waves:
  - A tool lists each fragment's possible parent structs and where its pointer comes from.
  - Coders read the code and give that pointer its real type, so the fragment becomes a field of its parent.
  - T2's suspect group of 53 types is judged this way too, not held.
- **Runs the judgment work at high effort.** The tracing and the twin reviews get high-effort experts, and coders on high.

**Naming moves to its own phase, 3.46.** Struct and field names come right after consolidation. File layout, the kit and validation each move down by one, to 3.47 to 3.49. I'll renumber the generation plan once you've approved the new plan.

**What stays the same:**
- all 218 files rebuild byte-identical;
- the type and signature checks pass, including the new parameter-type check;
- the Ghidra types are rewritten and pass the six proofs at the milestone check;
- no file moves;
- the phase ends with the docs task (story, retrospective, wiki, charts).

The background behind it (the shape count, the SOTN comparison and the record of what Gen 3 left unfinished) is in `/home/musashi/bfm-decomp/phase-ends/current/REPLAN.md`. I'll put the draft in the plan view when it's ready.

No, we didn't. I counted, and the casts are still there. They just changed form. Earlier phases turned the raw pointer arithmetic into struct casts, so code like `*(s16 *)((u8 *)p + 0x94)` now reads `((Unkstruct_8012ACA0 *)arg0)->unk94`. That's easier to read, but the cast is still at every use.

| | Our source | Symphony of the Night (SOTN) |
|---|---|---|
| `.c` files | 4,121 | 3,362 |
| Struct casts at the point of use | 261,044, in 2,633 files | about 7,783 |
| Raw pointer-arithmetic casts | 5,569 | 5 |

Our count includes the shared copies, so it overstates a little, but the gap is still huge.

**How SOTN handles a 2-byte field at offset 0x10.** It doesn't make a small struct for it. The field lives inside the real struct, even when nobody knows what it is yet: SOTN still has about 12,500 reads of fields named like `unk10`. What it doesn't have is the cast.
- **One typed pointer per function.** Every enemy function takes `Entity *self`, so a read is just `self->unk10`.
- **Per-enemy overlays for the differences.** Data that varies between enemies sits in a per-enemy layout over a spare area of the actor struct, read as `self->ext.<enemy>.<field>`. That accounts for about 17,000 reads.
- **A union where the shipped game really used one pointer as two types.**

The lesson for us: an unknown field name is fine, a fragment struct plus a cast is not. Readability comes from giving the pointer its type, not from naming every field.

**Removing the casts is now part of the 3.45 replan.** I sent this to the planner:
- **Measure the casts.** The milestone counts the casts left at the point of use. The target is zero wherever the pointer's source can be given a type.
- **When a cast may stay.** A cast is recorded and kept only where the game itself used one pointer as two types (a union is preferred there), or where the bytes refuse after the usual compiler tricks.
- **The raw pointer-arithmetic casts are in scope too.** All 5,569 become field accesses.
- **The README graph shows the casts dropping.**

This is the same tracing work as absorbing the fragments. Once a pointer has its type, the fragment and its casts disappear together.

Agreed. That's now the bar for the whole codebase, and the 3.45 replan is being drafted against it.

In SOTN terms, it means four things:
- **Organized structs.** Each real thing in the game, such as an actor, the camera or a menu, gets one struct. Data that differs between kinds of actor goes inside that struct, as SOTN does with its per-enemy overlays. Fragment structs go away.
- **Typed pointers.** A function that works on an actor takes an `Actor *`, so the code reads `actor->unk10` with no cast.
- **No unneeded casts.** A cast stays only where the shipped game really used one pointer as two types, and each one is recorded with its reason.
- **Unknown field names are fine.** A field can stay `unkNN` inside a real struct until something proves its meaning. Fragment structs are not fine.

I've written the bar onto the project card, which every agent reads. The planner has it as the phase's standard, and the docs task will add it to the Gen 3 standards page.

One housekeeping slip: the card commit also took in six research reports that were already staged. They were meant to be committed anyway, so nothing is lost or wrong.

**What happened.** I checked the mod's own state files:
- **05:19:03:** your new Claude Code session started, and PA3's startup hook hit an error: its tools weren't available yet because the session hadn't finished loading.
- **05:19:22:** that error made PA3 start a "repair" update by itself. It's not a new version, just a reinstall to fix the error.
- **05:19:30:** the repair finished. Its log ends with "pa3_update: done".
- **But** the marker that says "an update is running" was never cleared. It still says "running" now, 12 minutes later.

The mod holds every release while that marker says an update is running. That's why my request to resume T14 got "waiting: a PA3 update is running". So when I told you an update was installing, I was relaying the mod's own wrong status. I should have checked it first.

**Two smaller points:**
- T14 was cut off at 05:19 after only reading files, before it changed anything, so nothing is damaged.
- I also released a talk hold that was still set.

**What I recommend.** Set that one marker file (`.run/mod/update.json`) to "done" by hand. That's a one-line change in PA3's own state file, so I want your OK. The queued resume should then go through and T14 restarts from its note. Separately, I'll draft a bug report for PA3: a repair update that finishes still leaves its "running" marker, and that blocks every release afterwards.

T14 is running again. Clearing the stale marker unblocked it: the mod restarted T14's expert from its progress note.

**What happened when I cleared it:**
- **The mod reported its repair as finished.** It said the installed release was restored, which is the same PA3 3.32.18 you already had. It printed the project's version as "?", a small second glitch that's in the report.
- **It restarted T14 itself.** It decided T14 had been cut off by the session ending, not by your stop, so it ran a fresh expert from the progress note. That expert picks up from the reading it had done.
- **My own queued resume was refused as no longer needed.**

**The cause, in short.** When your new session started, PA3's startup hook ran before Claude Code had finished loading and threw an error. PA3 took that as "the mod is broken" and ran a reinstall by itself. The reinstall finished in 8 seconds, but it left its "update running" marker set, and that marker blocks every release. Nothing you did caused it, and killing T14 was fine: it hadn't changed anything yet.

**The bug report** is drafted at `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-musashi-bfm-decomp/252d32b5-eb3b-4ca8-9931-8e47bb99cd41/scratchpad/pa3-bug-stale-repair-marker.md`.
